claims.text: Population structure is the make-up of a population by age groups and sex, shown on an age/sex pyramid: the bars are age groups, males on one side and females on the other, and the shape is a record of the birth and death rates a country has had.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A structure answer names the broad groups and their proportions, young dependants (0-14), the economically active (15-64) and elderly dependants (65 and over), rather than only the pyramid's outline, because a structure is the groups and their shares, not the silhouette alone.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A wide-based pyramid, with a large share of children, comes from a high birth rate and a growing population; a narrow-based pyramid with a top-heavy shape comes from a low birth rate and an ageing population.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An age group's share of the population is males plus females in that group; reading one bar or one side of the pyramid undercounts it.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The dependent population is the people too young or too old to work, who rely on the economically active; the dependency ratio compares dependants with people of working age, so a high ratio means each worker supports more people.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A high dependent population, whether mostly young or mostly old, shifts a country's spending towards schools and clinics or towards pensions and care, because the active group must fund both its own households and the dependants'.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Niger has one of the world's highest dependent populations: nearly half its people are under 15 (around 44 per cent in the early 2020s) against a small economically active share, so the dependency ratio is high and each worker supports many children.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Niger's young structure comes from its high birth rate, around 45 per 1000 in the early 2020s, which keeps adding large cohorts of children while the adult group stays thin, because fertility has not yet fallen.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The implications for Niger are a school-age cohort too large for the classrooms and teachers available, clinics stretched by child and maternal care, and too few adults to fund it all, since around 44 per cent of the population is under 15.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).
